title: Arlo and the Deep River Rescue
markdown:
Arlo the otter had quick paws, quicker whiskers, and a secret that made him feel smaller than a pebble in a rush. He was king of the shallows. Splash-dam champion? That was him. The deep dark water sent shivers down his spine. His tummy did a frantic samba. His brave heart shrank to a ladybug. He’d rather chase dragonflies in puddles than dip a paw where he couldn’t feel the bottom.

A frantic cry: “Arlo! My toolbox! It’s gone adrift!” Old Gwyn the lock keeper, beard flowing like a white waterfall. This was not just any box. Inside, a tiny gleaming brass gear — the heart of Gwyn’s mighty lock gate. Arlo’s sharp eyes spotted it, bobbing a whisker too far. He paddled, heart thrumming. He stretched… and missed. Plop. The toolbox spun, caught the current, and raced toward the gurgling maw of the Whispering Rapids. Arlo’s fur stood on end. The Rapids. The deep dark Rapids.

“Hold on, Arlo!” Clank-clank-clank. Cressida the clockwork duck gleamed, springs and gears, a winding key, a determined tick-tock. “That gear is vital! We must get it back!”

A waddle and a splash. “Hop on! Adventure awaits!” Arlo gulped. Whiskers twitched. Gwyn’s silent lock gate and Cressida’s steady clanking spurred him. He scrambled onto her metallic back. Gears whirred like tiny bees.

Downstream they sped, a blur of green and brown. “Faster!” Arlo squeaked, pointing. The toolbox was a speck, too close to the roar. Then a mossy obstacle: Bartholomew, a grumpy beaver with teeth like chisels, dam a fortress of sticks and mud. “No one shall pass!”

“Oh, fiddlesticks,” Cressida clanked. “A detour! Through the Tangled Thicket!” Brambles clawed. Mud sucked. Squelch, splash, snag. A slow sticky crawl. Bartholomew chuckled from his dam.

They burst back onto the river, dripping. The toolbox sat perilously close to churning white water. “Here’s where it gets interesting,” Cressida said, gears picking up. “The current is like a giant hand. You’ll need to swim beside me, in the deep.”

Arlo’s stomach performed a triple backflip. The Rapids’ roar was a deafening hiss. Icy chill prickled his fur. The water was a dizzying dark swirl of foam.

“I… I can’t,” he whispered.

“Arlo.” Her voice firm. “That gear is important. Sometimes the bravest thing is facing what makes your whiskers quiver.”

He looked at her unwavering gaze, then the bobbing box. He took a breath of damp earth and panic. Then, with a yelp more determined than terrified, he plunged. Cold was a slap. He kicked. Forced his paws. The current seized, tugged, pulled. Down. He kicked harder, picturing her steady clank. He was swimming in the deep. Strong water, yes. If he kept moving, he could manage.

He gained on the toolbox. Then a sharp twang, a grinding crunch. Past a sunken log, Cressida’s key snagged. She lurched. Gears froze. “Oh, dear. My key… I’m stuck!” The box was strokes away, heading for the thundering fall. Arlo knew. He had to go on alone.

“I’ll get it! Hold on!” He poured otter speed into the swim. Spray stung. He reached the toolbox as it teetered. A tremendous heave nudged it away. He pushed, guided it toward calmer water at the falls’ base.

Exhausted, exhilarated, he brought it to the bank. Gwyn stood beaming. “You found it! And the gear! You wonderful otter!” As Gwyn secured the box, Cressida, free of the snag, clanked toward them, gears merry again.

The deep water was still deep. It was not a monster. The old lock gate creaked open with a groan, and Arlo’s chest held something warm that did not need a name. He shook the Rapids out of his whiskers and, for the first time, did not mind that he could not feel the bottom.
